items.title: Ted Piltzecker interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 10, 2019
items.q: When I was at Eastman Marian McPartland came through with her trio. It was Rick Petrone and Joe Corsello the other members. And they gave a little workshop and I sat in on the vibraphone

ctx.x: No. I like this stuff. Because other people will like it, not just music fans, other profs etcetera. Okay. So you’ve got a long list of people that have played with you and people that you’ve played with and I wanted to ask you about how George Shearing came into your life.

It sort of was a surprise. When I was at Eastman Marian McPartland came through with her trio. It was Rick Petrone and Joe Corsello the other members. And they gave a little workshop and I sat in on the vibraphone and that was — to call it basic would be a polite description. I mean I didn’t know anything. I was pretty Neanderthal on the instrument at that time. I learned, I got more finesse later. But she remembered it, so George needed a vibraphone player for a quintet a year or two later and I guess he called…

[percussive scats], as you know the way he would play is [percussive scats], but this was continuing, right, and the whole front line had to do that together. So George would be playing this lock hand position and the vibraphone and guitar had to play absolute unison with that, in that kind of — and there’s no way, it’s impossible. So you learn to listen in a really intense way. And after one or two times, and you didn’t rehearse. It was like the first, I’m doing this, there’s an audience and we’re trying to like…
